common_name: Cinderella's Carriage Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Hybrid Flat Heirloom-Type Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Cinderella's Carriage is an AAS-winning hybrid version of the classic flattened, deep-orange Cinderella-type pumpkin, bred for powdery mildew resistance and higher, more reliable yields than the older open-pollinated heirloom.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vigorous vines ample room to spread. Cinderella's Carriage is an AAS-winning hybrid take on the classic Cinderella-type pumpkin — the flattened, deeply ribbed, deep-orange-red fruit famously associated with the Rouge Vif d'Etampes heirloom — bred to add meaningful powdery mildew resistance and more consistent, higher yields than the older open-pollinated version, while keeping the same striking flattened silhouette prized for fall display. Fruit reaches 15-25 pounds with dense, good-flavored flesh usable for cooking as well as decoration. Because it is naturally more disease-resistant than the heirloom, the vines tend to stay productive and healthy later into the season in humid climates. Harvest when the rind hardens and color deepens fully, cutting the stem rather than pulling to avoid damaging the fruit, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing.
sources: All-America Selections — Cinderella's Carriage Pumpkin winner announcement

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil; Sorcerer is an AAS-winning semi-bush pumpkin producing uniform 10-12 pound classic jack-o-lantern fruit on a much more compact vine than traditional sprawling pumpkin varieties.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun. Sorcerer is an AAS-winning jack-o-lantern pumpkin bred with a semi-bush habit, taking noticeably less garden space than traditional sprawling pumpkin vines while still producing a full-size crop of classic round, deep-orange, 10-12 pound carving pumpkins with the strong, smooth handle and even shape prized for jack-o-lanterns. Its more compact vine makes it a practical choice for smaller vegetable gardens that still want to grow real carving-size pumpkins rather than miniatures. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and the color deepens to solid orange, cutting the stem with a few inches attached rather than pulling it, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two to improve storage life before Halloween display.

common_name: Baby Bear Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Small Hull-Less-Seed Pie Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Baby Bear is an AAS-winning small pie pumpkin prized both for sweet baking flesh and for its hull-less, easy-to-roast seeds.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Baby Bear is an AAS-winning small pie pumpkin, producing round, deep-orange fruit around 1.5 pounds each with sweet, fine-grained, good-baking flesh well suited to pies, soups, and purees, and small enough to make an attractive miniature carving or decorative pumpkin as well. Its standout feature is hull-less (naked) seeds — unlike most pumpkins, the seeds lack the tough outer hull, so they can be roasted and eaten whole with no shelling required, making Baby Bear a favorite for gardeners who want a dual-purpose crop of both good-eating flesh and easy snacking seeds from the same fruit. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and color deepens, cutting the stem with a few inches attached, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before use or storage.
sources: All-America Selections — Baby Bear Pumpkin winner announcement

common_name: Pepitas Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Hull-Less Seed Snacking Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Pepitas is an AAS-winning pumpkin bred specifically for its naked, hull-less seeds, harvested and roasted for snacking rather than grown primarily for the flesh.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Pepitas is an AAS-winning pumpkin bred specifically as a seed crop — the medium-orange fruit is filled with abundant naked, hull-less green seeds (the same type sold commercially as pepitas), which can be scooped out, rinsed, and roasted directly with no shelling needed, unlike the tough-hulled seeds of most pumpkin varieties. It is a fun, productive choice for gardeners who want a real harvest of roastable snacking seeds without buying store pepitas, and the flesh, while secondary to the seed crop, is still usable in cooking. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and the vine begins to decline, then scoop and separate the seeds from the pulp before rinsing and roasting or drying them for storage.
sources: All-America Selections — Pepitas Pumpkin winner announcement

common_name: Orange Smoothie Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Smooth-Rind Small Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Orange Smoothie is an AAS-winning small pumpkin bred for an unusually smooth, rib-free rind, unlike the deep ridges typical of most jack-o-lantern and pie pumpkins.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Orange Smoothie is an AAS-winning small-to-medium pumpkin distinguished by an unusually smooth, nearly rib-free rind — most pumpkins have pronounced vertical ridges, but Orange Smoothie's clean, rounded surface gives it a distinctive look for decoration and makes it especially easy to carve or paint without ridges interrupting the design. The fruit is a good size for both decorative use and cooking, with reasonably good flesh quality for pies and purees. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and color deepens to solid orange, cutting the stem with a few inches attached, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before use or fall display.
sources: All-America Selections — Orange Smoothie Pumpkin winner announcement
